newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodian PM says some fear Pol Pot testimony.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian PM says some fear Pol Pot testimony.

text.p: Cambodian Co-Premier Prince Norodom Ranariddh said on Monday some people and countries feared what captured Khmer Rouge leader Pol Pot might say if he appeared in court as pressure grew to bring the hated strongman to justice.
The prince insisted the guerrilla leader was still alive and said those saying he was already dead had no interest in seeing him testify before a court.
"It appears to me that some Cambodians, and maybe some countries, are not really willing for Pol Pot to be alive and be brought to justice," the prince told reporters.
"Pol Pot will say -- those people are involved, those countries supported me for years."

The prince did not elaborate on which people or countries might be afraid of Pol Pot testifying in court but few political players in Cambodia, including the prince himself, have not, at one time or another, been allied with Pol Pot's Khmer Rouge.

While Cambodians waited to see if they would get a glimpse of Pol Pot, the United States stepped up efforts to bring the architect of the "killing fields" rule to court to answer for crimes against humanity.

The New York Times reported on Monday that U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright had asked Canadian Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy to request the extradition of Pol Pot from Cambodia to face an international tribunal. Only Canada and Denmark have laws permitting them to make such a request, the Times said.
The Canadian Embassy in Phnom Penh said it had yet to be informed of the decision.
But even as pressure mounted for a war crimes tribunal, many analysts doubted whether Pol Pot would ever be brought to trial.
"I'm rather sceptical he'll ever see the light of day," said a diplomat.
Ranariddh's co-premier and political rival Hun Sen said on Sunday that he had an unconfirmed report that Pol Pot was dead.

But several hours later the prince's top military adviser, deputy chief of general staff Nhiek Bun Chhay, returned from northern Cambodia saying he had seen Pol Pot that morning and the breakaway Khmer Rouge faction detaining him would hand him over to authorities soon.
Nhiek Bun Chhay has been negotiating with the Khmer Rouge breakaway faction that broke with Pol Pot earlier this month.

Last week the two prime ministers sent a letter to the United Nations asking for the world body's assistance in bringing to justice those responsible for the crimes committed during the 1975-79 Khmer Rouge reign of terror.
It was the first time in months that the two feuding premiers had acted in unison on the Khmer Rouge issue.

The long-running row between the two over power-sharing and the fate of Pol Pot simmered on Monday, with the prince hinting that he favoured an amnesty for the leader of the Khmer Rouge breakaway faction, Khieu Samphan, if Pol Pot was brought to justice.
Last week, Hun Sen declared negotiations with the Khmer Rouge illegal and told Ranariddh to decide between working with him in their fractured coalition or siding with the rebels.
Pol Pot fled his Anlong Veng headquarters earlier this month after ordering the execution of his defence chief and almost a dozen of his family members.
The renegade Khmer Rouge faction captured Pol Pot last Thursday but Ranariddh did not say when he expected the group to hand him over to the government.
More than a million Cambodians died of starvation, disease and hard labour, or were executed as enemies of the Khmer Rouge during Pol Pot's rule.
